lessons.title: Estimating the size of cell structures
lessons.text:
## Estimating the size of cell structures
LV: GCSE · Foundation
S: Cells and the structures inside them are far too small to measure with a ruler, so biologists use magnification, unit conversions and quick estimates to work out how big they are compared with each other.
O: Calculate magnification, image size or real size, converting both lengths to the same unit first
O: Estimate the relative size or area of structures inside a cell, and explain when an estimate is the right tool
O: Write very small sizes using the prefixes milli, micro and nano and using standard form
REQ: aqa-gcse-biology:4.1.1.2.e @1,2,3
T: magnification | How many times bigger an image appears than the real object, found by dividing image size by real size
T: order of magnitude | A comparison of sizes to the nearest power of ten, used for rough estimates
T: standard form | A number written as a value between 1 and 10 multiplied by a power of ten, useful for very small sizes
T: field of view | The circular area you can see when you look down the eyepiece of a microscope
H: Units for very small things
P: Cell structures are measured in tiny units. A **millimetre** (mm) is a thousandth of a metre, a **micrometre** is a thousandth of a millimetre, and a **nanometre** is a thousandth of a micrometre. So 1 mm is 1000 micrometres. A **centimetre** is a hundredth of a metre.
P: Very small real sizes are often written in **standard form**, for example 3.7 × 10^{-2} mm instead of 0.037 mm. Examiners may expect an answer in this form when the real size is very small.
H: The magnification equation
E: magnification = image size ÷ real size :: how many times bigger the image is than the object
P: You can rearrange it to find either missing quantity: real size is image size divided by magnification, and image size is real size multiplied by magnification.
K: Before you divide, put the image size and the real size in the same unit. Converting between millimetres and micrometres (multiply or divide by 1000) is the step where most marks are lost.
X: An image of a cell is 50 mm wide. The real cell is 2000 micrometres wide. What is the magnification?
> Convert the real size to millimetres: 2000 ÷ 1000 = 2, so the real cell is 2 mm wide.
> Divide image size by real size: 50 ÷ 2 = 25.
> The magnification is ×25. Magnification has no unit because the two lengths cancel.
X: A structure is 4 micrometres across and is drawn at a magnification of ×1500. How wide is it in the drawing, in millimetres?
> Multiply real size by magnification: 4 × 1500 = 6000, so the image is 6000 micrometres wide.
> Convert to millimetres: 6000 ÷ 1000 = 6.
> The structure is 6 mm wide in the drawing.
!: Mixing up magnification and resolution. Magnification makes an image bigger; resolution is how clearly two points that are close together can be seen as separate.
H: Estimating relative size and area
P: Sometimes you don't need an exact size, or you can't measure one. You only want to know roughly how big one structure is compared with another. An **estimate** gives a quick, rough answer that is good enough for that job.
- **Count across:** see how many of the smaller structure would fit in a line across the larger one, then state the result as a rough ratio.
- **Use the field of view as a ruler:** if you know how wide the field of view is, count how many cells fit across it and divide.
- **Think in powers of ten:** say whether one thing is about 10, 100 or 1000 times bigger than another. This is an order-of-magnitude comparison.
X: Suppose the field of view is 2 mm across and about 10 cells fit across it in a line. Estimate the width of one cell, then compare it with a structure about 2 micrometres wide.
> Each cell is about 2 ÷ 10 = 0.2 mm wide.
> Convert to micrometres: 0.2 × 1000 = 200, so each cell is roughly 200 micrometres across.
> Compare: 200 ÷ 2 = 100, so the cell is about 100 times wider than the structure, two orders of magnitude bigger.
P: Area grows faster than width. If about 5 of a structure fit across a cell, then roughly 5 × 5 = 25 of them would cover the same flat area, so its area is about one twenty-fifth of the cell's.
K: Use an estimate when you need a quick comparison rather than an exact measurement, when you cannot measure directly, or to check that a calculated answer is the right order of magnitude.
!: Assuming that a structure five times narrower takes up a fifth of the area. Area depends on width times width, so it is closer to a twenty-fifth.
D: bio-animal-cell
DNEED: A microscope field of view drawn as a circle with a 2 mm scale across it and a row of about ten cells spanning the diameter, to show the field of view used as a ruler
GAP: The brief gives no typical real sizes for organelles such as nuclei, mitochondria or chloroplasts, so the lesson cannot compare named sub-cellular structures with real figures
SUM: Magnification equals image size divided by real size, and both lengths must be in the same unit first.
SUM: One millimetre is 1000 micrometres, and very small sizes can be written in standard form.
SUM: An estimate compares sizes roughly, by counting how many fit across or by using powers of ten.
SUM: A structure that is five times narrower has roughly a twenty-fifth of the area, not a fifth.
SRC: AQA, GCSE Biology 8461 specification, Cell biology subject content | standard | 2026-11-25 | https://www.aqa.org.uk/subjects/science/gcse/biology-8461/specification/subject-content/cell-biology
SRC: Save My Exams, Microscopy (AQA GCSE Biology) revision note | secondary | 2026-11-25 | https://www.savemyexams.com/gcse/biology/aqa/18/revision-notes/1-cell-biology/1-1-cell-structure/1-1-5-microscopy/
SRC: MyEdSpace, Calculations of magnification, real size and image size | secondary | 2026-11-25 | https://myedspace.co.uk/myresources/gcse/biology/aqa/revision-notes/calculations-of-magnification-real-size-and-image-size
Q: What is the equation for magnification? | Magnification equals image size divided by real size.
Q: How many micrometres are in one millimetre? | 1000 micrometres.
Q: What must you do before using the magnification equation? | Put the image size and the real size into the same unit.
Q: When is an estimate useful in cell biology? | When you need a quick rough comparison of sizes, cannot measure directly, or want to check a calculated answer.
Q: What is the difference between magnification and resolution? | Magnification is how much bigger the image is; resolution is how clearly two close points can be told apart.
M1@1: An image is 30 mm wide and the real object is 3 mm wide. What is the magnification? | ×10 | ×90 | ×33 | ×0.1 | Magnification is image size divided by real size, and 30 ÷ 3 = 10, so the image is ten times bigger.
M1@3: How many micrometres are there in 0.5 mm? | 500 micrometres | 50 micrometres | 5000 micrometres | 0.0005 micrometres | There are 1000 micrometres in each millimetre, so multiply 0.5 by 1000 to get 500 micrometres.
M2@1: An image is 40 mm wide and the real cell is 100 micrometres wide. What is the magnification? | ×400 | ×0.4 | ×4 | ×2.5 | Convert first: 100 micrometres is 0.1 mm. Then 40 ÷ 0.1 = 400. Dividing 40 by 100 without converting gives the wrong answer.
M2@2: About 8 mitochondria could fit in a line across a cell. Which is the best estimate of the cell's width compared with one mitochondrion? | About 8 times wider | About 64 times wider | About 80 times wider | About the same width | Counting how many fit across gives the ratio of widths directly, so the cell is roughly 8 times wider.
M3@2: About 4 of a structure fit in a line across a cell. Roughly how many would it take to cover the same flat area as the cell? | About 16 | About 4 | About 8 | About 40 | Area depends on width times width, so roughly 4 × 4 = 16 of them would cover the cell's flat area.
M3@1,3: A cell drawn at ×400 is 14.8 mm wide in the image. What is its real width? | 37 micrometres | 5920 micrometres | 3.7 micrometres | 370 micrometres | Real size is image size divided by magnification: 14.8 ÷ 400 = 0.037 mm, and 0.037 × 1000 = 37 micrometres.
SA2@2: Explain when a biologist would estimate the size of a sub-cellular structure rather than measure it, and describe one way to make the estimate. | An estimate is used when an exact measurement is not needed or not possible, for a quick comparison of sizes, or to check a calculated answer is sensible. One method is to count how many of the structure would fit across the cell and give the result as a rough ratio. | Exact value not needed or not possible ; Quick comparison or checking an answer ; Describes counting across or field of view method ; Gives result as a ratio or order of magnitude

lessons.title: Required practical: observing cells with a light microscope
lessons.text:
## Required practical: observing cells with a light microscope
LV: GCSE · Foundation
S: Looking at real plant and animal cells under a light microscope, then drawing and labelling what you see, is one of the required practicals in AQA GCSE Biology and builds the skills examiners test on microscopy.
O: Use a light microscope in the right order to bring cells into clear focus
O: Make a clear, labelled biological drawing that includes a magnification scale
O: Work out the real size of a cell from its image size and the magnification
REQ: aqa-gcse-biology:4.1.1.2.RP1 @1,2,3
T: magnification | How many times bigger an image appears than the real object, found by dividing image size by real size
T: field of view | The circular area you can see when you look down the eyepiece of a microscope
T: biological drawing | A clear scientific record of a specimen, drawn with single lines and labels rather than shading
H: Using the microscope
P: This practical builds two of the practical skills AQA lists: using apparatus and using a light microscope well. You look at a selection of cells from plants and from animals and record them as drawings.
- Start with the **lowest-power objective lens**, so you can find the cells easily in a wide field of view.
- Focus the image, then move to a **higher-power** objective lens to see more detail.
- You can compare what you see with micrographs, photographs or video of the same kinds of cell.
K: Always begin on the lowest-power objective lens and only then move to higher power.
SAFE: Follow your teacher's instructions and your school's risk assessment when handling slides, glass and any stains or specimens.
H: Drawing what you see
P: A biological drawing is a scientific record, not a piece of art. Examiners want to see what is really there, clearly.
- Draw large, using most of the space on the page.
- Use clear, single, continuous lines.
- Do not shade or colour in.
- Label the structures you can see.
- Add a **magnification scale** to every drawing; this is required for the practical.
!: Shading and sketchy lines make a drawing look artistic but lose marks. Use clean single lines and labels only.
D: bio-plant-cell
D: bio-animal-cell
DNEED: A labelled light microscope showing the eyepiece, objective lenses, stage and focusing knobs, with an arrow showing the move from low to high power
H: From drawing to real size
E: real size = image size ÷ magnification :: rearranged from magnification = image size ÷ real size
X: An onion cell viewed at ×400 is 14.8 mm wide in your image. How wide is the real cell?
> Divide image size by magnification: 14.8 ÷ 400 = 0.037, so the real cell is 0.037 mm wide.
> Convert to micrometres: 0.037 × 1000 = 37.
> The real cell is about 37 micrometres wide, or 3.7 × 10^{-2} mm in standard form.
!: Forgetting to convert units. Put both lengths in the same unit before you divide, then give the answer in the unit asked for.
!: The specification point number for this practical differs between resources: it appears here under 4.1.1.2, but some revision material lists it under 4.1.1.5. Check the current AQA specification for the reference your school uses.
GAP: The brief does not cover how to prepare and stain a slide, which stains to use, or which specific cells to observe, so these practical steps are not taught here
SUM: Find cells on the lowest-power objective lens first, then switch to higher power for detail.
SUM: A biological drawing uses clear single lines, no shading, labels and a magnification scale.
SUM: Real size equals image size divided by magnification, after converting both lengths to the same unit.
SRC: AQA, GCSE Biology 8461 specification, Cell biology subject content | standard | 2026-11-25 | https://www.aqa.org.uk/subjects/science/gcse/biology-8461/specification/subject-content/cell-biology
SRC: Save My Exams, Required Practical: Microscopy (AQA GCSE Biology) revision note | secondary | 2026-11-25 | https://www.savemyexams.com/gcse/biology/aqa/18/revision-notes/1-cell-biology/1-1-cell-structure/1-1-6-required-practical-microscopy
SRC: Save My Exams, Microscopy (AQA GCSE Biology) revision note | secondary | 2026-11-25 | https://www.savemyexams.com/gcse/biology/aqa/18/revision-notes/1-cell-biology/1-1-cell-structure/1-1-5-microscopy/
Q: Which objective lens should you start with? | The lowest-power objective lens, then move to higher power.
Q: What must every drawing in the microscopy practical include? | A magnification scale, as well as labels.
Q: Should a biological drawing be shaded? | No. Use clear single lines and labels with no shading.
Q: How do you find the real size of a cell from its image? | Divide the image size by the magnification, with both in the same unit.
M1@1: Which objective lens should you use first when looking at a new slide? | The lowest-power lens | The highest-power lens | Any lens, it does not matter | The medium-power lens | Starting on low power gives a wide field of view, so the cells are easier to find before you zoom in.
M1@2: Which feature should a biological drawing of cells include? | Labels and a magnification scale | Careful shading to show depth | Colour to match the stain used | Sketchy lines to show texture | Biological drawings are scientific records, so they need labels and a scale, not artistic shading or colour.
M2@2: A student's drawing is small, shaded and has no labels. Which change would improve it most for the practical? | Redraw it large with single lines, labels and a scale | Add more shading to make it look realistic | Colour it in to show the different structures | Trace a textbook photo instead of the slide | A good drawing is large, uses clear single lines, is labelled and includes a magnification scale.
M2@3: A cell is 12 mm wide in an image at ×200. What is its real width? | 60 micrometres | 2400 micrometres | 6 micrometres | 600 micrometres | Real size is 12 ÷ 200 = 0.06 mm, and 0.06 × 1000 = 60 micrometres.
M3@1,3: A student finds cells on high power, measures an image 20 mm wide at ×100 and gives the real size as 0.2 micrometres. What went wrong? | They began on high power and gave 0.2 mm as micrometres | They used the right lens order and made no unit error | They should have multiplied 20 by 100 to find real size | They should start on high power and the answer is correct | They should start on low power, and 20 ÷ 100 = 0.2 mm, which is 200 micrometres, not 0.2 micrometres.
SA2@2: Describe how to produce a good biological drawing of cells seen under a light microscope. | Draw large on the page using clear, single, continuous lines with no shading. Label the visible structures and include a magnification scale on the drawing. | Large drawing ; Single clear lines ; No shading ; Labels ; Magnification scale
